doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Bad arrangements, 'make it work', and the Pepsi commercial
summary: Raph recalls weak arrangers and copyists, Charlie Calello's 'Make it work', and a Pepsi commercial where he invented horn fills over eight hours.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Did you ever have to deal with bad arrangers, bad copyists, those things?

Constantly. You had to make them sound good. There was one expression that Charlie Calello, who was one of the successful arrangers, used to use and that was, “Make it work.” I said, “Well Charlie, this is impractical.” He said, “Make it work” you know. So you made it work.
Yeah. You might find something different to play that’s not on the paper.

There were even times, and many times, when we went into a date and there might have been some sketched music but certainly not an arrangement. Or there might have been no music and they just said look we’re doing this and they played a little bit of the rhythm for us, live, and we were to make up some horn fills. And I remember doing a Pepsi Cola commercial that way, where the band was a successful rock & roll band that Pepsi decided they should do the next commercial because they were hot. And these guys had

three or four solid days of studio time. I came in, my segment took about eight hours. And we just sat there making up things and discarding things, and keeping a note here and a chord there. And it was the most boring way to do it but the money was good so you didn’t mind.
I guess Pepsi had the money to spend at the time, right?
